e.t: This Greek LXX verb means “unwilling”: it describes someone who does not desire or consent to do something. It presents reluctance or a refusal of willingness, rather than naming a person or object. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament represented here, at 1 Samuel 24:11. Its exact force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic meaning remains the absence of willingness to act.

This noun means “wildness” or “savageness”—a quality marked by being untamed, fierce, or lacking gentleness. It describes the character or condition of something wild rather than naming a specific action. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 15:21. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense is the presence of wild or savage character.

Azōr is a proper name, rendered “Azor.” It identifies a named individual or place rather than expressing a general idea, action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, the name occurs twice: once in Joshua 19:45 and once in Jeremiah 35:1. Without the surrounding verse text, the available information establishes the name’s identity but does not determine whether each occurrence refers to a person or a place. Its meaning is therefore best understood as the proper name Azor.

This noun refers to something pointed. Its basic idea is a sharp or tapering point rather than a broad or rounded form. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs only once, in Proverbs 32:18, so its precise reference there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. The available meaning is clear, but the single occurrence gives no wider range of uses to compare. This word belongs to the Greek LXX vocabulary and should remain distinct from similarly rendered words in other biblical language corpora.

This noun refers to “anything used for anointing,” including “hog's-lard.” It names a substance used in anointing rather than the action itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears four times, with one occurrence each in Exodus, Job, Ezekiel, and Micah. Its precise significance in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its basic sense is an anointing substance or material.

This word refers to a sweet cake, a noun naming a prepared food rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 16:3. Its central sense is directly defined as “sweet cake,” and the English rendering there is cake. Since the verse text is not included here, the word’s exact role in that sentence must be understood from the surrounding passage. Its ordinary lexical meaning, however, is a sweet cake.

This word describes something adverse or opposed—something that stands against or works contrary to another person, thing, or purpose. It functions as a noun in the Greek LXX corpus and points to opposition rather than agreement or support. The word occurs once, in Sirach 37:9. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and its immediate context.

This Greek LXX verb means “open up”: it describes making something open or accessible, whether an entrance, an opening, or something that was previously closed. It can refer to the act of opening rather than to the object itself. The word occurs 153 times in the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, showing a broad, ordinary use for opening something. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what is being opened and the surrounding sentence.

This verb means “forbid”: to say that something must not be done or is not permitted. It expresses a clear prohibition rather than a suggestion or personal preference. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 1:34. The surrounding verse text is needed to identify exactly what is being forbidden there, but the word itself describes the act of prohibiting or refusing permission.

This Greek LXX verb means to “chase away”—to drive someone or something off rather than allow it to remain. It describes an action carried out against another person or thing. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, in Lamentations 3:43. Since the verse text and surrounding passage are not provided here, the word’s exact force in that sentence must be understood from its context.

This Greek LXX verb means “release; dismiss.” It describes sending someone away, letting someone go, or ending an obligation that keeps a person present or bound. The central idea is separation by permission: someone is released from a place, duty, claim, or continuing association. It occurs 22 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, so its exact force depends on what or whom the sentence says is being released or dismissed.

This noun means “rebel”—a person who turns against authority or resists it. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears twice, both in Ezra 4, so its recorded use is limited rather than broad. The word identifies someone by opposition, but the exact force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage. As a noun, it names the person who rebels rather than expressing the act itself.

This word means “origin” or “beginning,” referring to where something starts or to its earliest point. It is a noun used for the starting point of an event, period, or matter. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 215 times across 201 verses, from Genesis through Song of Songs, showing that it can describe beginnings in many settings. Its clearest rendering in the available passages is “beginning,” while the broader sense includes the idea of origin.

This Greek LXX verb means “high priest,” describing someone who serves or functions in that priestly role. It is a verb rather than simply a title, so it presents high-priestly service or action. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 4 Maccabees 4:18. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning is connected with being or acting as the high priest.

This verb means to abstain from food—to fast. It describes deliberately going without eating, often as an act of self-denial or urgent devotion. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs twice, once in Esther and once in 1 Maccabees. The central idea remains simple: a person refrains from food for a period of time. The surrounding passage is needed to understand the particular reason or purpose for fasting in each occurrence.

Astarta is a proper name, referring to a named figure or entity rather than describing an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, the name appears twice: once in Judges and once in 2 Chronicles. The available meaning is limited to the name itself, so its precise role in either passage must be understood from the surrounding verse and passage. It is distinctively preserved as “Astarta” in this Greek Old Testament word record.

This Greek LXX noun means “impassiveness; calmness”: a settled condition marked by freedom from agitation or disturbance. It describes an inward steadiness rather than an action. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at 4 Maccabees 8:26. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and argument, but its basic sense is remaining composed and undisturbed. It names a quality or state, not a person or event.

Baier is a proper name, referring to a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. The lexical gloss identifies the name as “Baiēr” and also gives “Vir.” In the Greek Old Testament, this word occurs once, in Judges 9:21. Without the verse text and surrounding passage, its specific role in that verse cannot be described further, but its basic function is clear: it identifies a particular person by name.

This noun refers to a gulf or pit—a deep, hollow, or sunken place. Its meaning can describe a physical depression or chasm, with the surrounding passage determining the precise picture intended. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Isaiah 14:23. The word itself points to depth and emptiness rather than to an action or a person. Its English rendering there is “pit,” which fits the basic sense of a deep or hollow place.

This Greek LXX verb means “pick up; bear.” It describes taking something up, carrying it, or bearing what has been placed upon someone. The central idea is active support or carrying, whether the object is physically lifted or something must be endured. It occurs five times in the Greek LXX, appearing in Judges, Ruth, 2 Kings, and Sirach. Its exact force in a particular passage depends on what is being carried or borne there.

This word is a proper name, given in the form “Bēthalamin” or “Vithalamin.” It identifies a specific named entity in the Greek Old Testament rather than expressing a general action, quality, or idea. It occurs once in the LXX, at 1 Kings 4:9. The name itself does not establish whether the named entity is a person, place, or other designation. Its precise referent depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

This noun means “threshold,” the entrance area at the base of a doorway. It refers to the boundary one crosses when entering or leaving a house or other place. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs only twice, in Jeremiah and the Epistle of Jeremiah. Its precise significance in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but its ordinary meaning remains the doorway’s threshold or entrance boundary.

The word means “wine-jar,” referring to a container used for holding wine. It is a noun, so it names the vessel itself rather than the drink or an action involving it. In the Greek Old Testament, this word occurs twice, both times in Jeremiah 19. Its precise significance in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its ordinary lexical meaning remains a wine-jar: a physical container associated with wine.

This word means “javelin,” a noun naming a weapon made for throwing. It refers to a pointed projectile used in scenes involving battle, attack, or defense. The word appears 14 times in the Greek Old Testament corpus, including passages from Exodus, Numbers, Joshua, 1 Samuel, Nehemiah, Jeremiah, and other books. Its basic meaning remains concrete and consistent: a javelin is the object being thrown or used as a weapon, while the surrounding verse determines the particular action or setting.

This word is a proper name identifying Byblioi, also given as Vivli. It is a name rather than a general description or action word. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Ezekiel 27:9. The name’s precise role in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its basic reference remains the named group or designation represented by Byblioi or Vivli. This is a Greek LXX word and should be understood as distinct from similarly rendered words in other biblical language corpora.

Gas is a proper name preserved in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies something named “Gas,” rather than describing an action, quality, or general object. The word appears once in the Greek Old Testament, at 2 Kings 18:35. Because the verse text and surrounding context are not available here, its precise referent in that passage cannot be stated more specifically without adding information beyond the word’s recorded meaning.

Gērsōni, also rendered Yirsoni, is a proper name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a named figure or group in the Greek Old Testament text. The name occurs three times in the LXX, appearing in two verses in 1 Chronicles: 1 Chronicles 26:21 and 1 Chronicles 29:8. Its specific identification depends on the surrounding passage, since the name itself functions primarily as a designation.

This word means “one must know,” expressing something that should be recognized or understood. It functions as an adjective, describing what is necessary to know rather than naming a person, object, or action. In the Greek LXX, it occurs once, in the Epistle of Jeremiah 1:51. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its basic sense is a matter that must be known.

This Greek LXX noun means “ring” or “circle,” describing a round shape or encircling form. It appears three times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical writings, including Job, Isaiah, and Sirach. In Job and Isaiah, it is rendered “circle,” supporting the sense of something round or forming a complete curve. Its exact force in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse and subject being described.

This adjective means “leather” and describes something made from or consisting of leather. It identifies the material associated with an object rather than expressing an action or quality such as strength or softness. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 14 times across 13 verses, including passages in Genesis, Leviticus, Numbers, and 2 Kings. Its precise application depends on the noun it describes in each passage.

This word means “elapse”. It is a verb describing time passing or a period coming to an end. In the Greek Old Testament tradition represented here, it appears once, in 2 Maccabees 11:26. That reference identifies where the word occurs, but without the verse text it does not establish a fuller context or special emphasis. Its basic sense remains simple: time elapses as it passes. The surrounding sentence determines precisely what period is being discussed.

This Greek LXX verb means “cut through.” It describes the act of breaking or making a way through something by cutting. The word appears 18 times in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books, so its basic sense is used across several narrative settings rather than being limited to one passage. Its precise force in any verse depends on what is being cut through, but the central idea remains cutting across or through an obstacle or material.

This verb means to guard something thoroughly and carefully, with attentive protection rather than casual oversight. In the Greek Old Testament, it describes the act of keeping a person, thing, or charge securely. It occurs 25 times across 25 verses, including passages from Genesis through 2 Maccabees. Its wording emphasizes careful preservation and faithful watchfulness, while the exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This Greek LXX verb means “go after; pursue,” describing active movement toward someone or something, often with the aim of catching or overtaking it. It can refer to following closely or pressing after a person. The word occurs 103 times in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books, showing a broad and recurring use for determined pursuit. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This Greek LXX verb means “encrypt; conceal”: it describes hiding something so that it is kept out of sight or not openly disclosed. As a verb, it expresses an action rather than a person, object, or quality. It occurs seven times in the Greek LXX corpus, including passages in Joshua, Proverbs, Ezekiel, Hosea, Amos, and 1 Maccabees. The surrounding verse determines whether the emphasis is on physically hiding something or keeping information concealed.

This noun means “praise” and can also carry the sense “common.” It names approval, commendation, or public recognition rather than describing an action by itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Proverbs 10:7, so its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. The word’s central idea is something spoken or recognized openly as worthy of approval, while its additional sense points to what is shared or common.

This verb means “break out/off”: it describes breaking something apart or away rather than merely moving it. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in the Septuagint rendering of Leviticus 1:17. Its exact force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but the basic idea remains an act of breaking away or separating. The word is action-oriented, expressing what someone does to something rather than naming an object, person, or quality.

This word means “myself,” referring back to the speaker or writer. It is a pronoun used when someone identifies himself as the person involved in an action, experience, or statement. The wording can emphasize personal involvement or distinguish the speaker from others. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 55 times, so it serves a recurring role in expressing what a person does, receives, or considers personally. Its exact force in a sentence depends on the surrounding words and context.

This Greek LXX verb means “continue”: to keep doing something or persist in an action. It describes ongoing activity rather than a single, completed act. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in Sirach 30:1. Because the verse text and surrounding context are not included here, its precise force in that passage must be understood from the sentence and larger passage, while its basic meaning remains the idea of continuing.

This Greek LXX verb means “empower”: to give someone strength, ability, or power to act. It describes an enabling action rather than merely describing a person’s existing strength. The word appears once in the Greek LXX, in Judges 6:34. Its exact force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning remains the act of empowering or strengthening someone for action.

This verb means to “feed upon,” describing the act of taking nourishment from something. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Job 40:30, so its basic sense is clear even though its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage. It expresses eating or feeding on a source of nourishment rather than merely approaching or touching it. The word functions as an action word, focusing attention on what is consumed.

This Greek LXX verb means to find out or discover something, especially when it becomes known through searching or investigation. It describes the action of coming upon knowledge that was not previously known. The word appears three times in the Greek LXX material represented here, all in the deuterocanonical books of Baruch and 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This adjective describes “getting under arms”—taking up weapons or preparing for armed action. It points to a person or group becoming armed, rather than to a weapon itself. In the LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 5:25. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included, the word’s precise force in that sentence cannot be stated beyond this basic idea.

This verb means “glean after the crop”—to gather what remains in a field after the main harvest has been collected. It describes a later gathering rather than the primary cutting of the crop. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, in Leviticus 19:10 and Deuteronomy 24:21, both within instructions concerning what remains after harvesting. Its exact force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and its larger instruction.

This LXX verb means “plan”: it describes intentionally forming a course of action. It presents planning as an active decision rather than a mere possibility or passing thought. The word occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament, once in Esther and once in Proverbs, so its normal lexical sense is clear even though the verse text is not included here. In each passage, the surrounding context determines what is being planned and how the action should be understood.

This verb means “send besides,” expressing the act of sending something or someone in addition to another. It describes an added sending rather than merely sending in isolation. The word appears three times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings preserved in this corpus: once in Proverbs and once each in Wisdom and 3 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what is being sent and what it is added to.

This noun means “supervisor”: a person appointed to oversee people, work, or responsibilities. It identifies someone charged with watching over a task or group rather than someone merely participating in it. In the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books, it occurs 13 times, including passages in Numbers, Judges, Kings, Chronicles, Nehemiah, and 1 Maccabees. Its precise responsibility depends on the surrounding passage, but the central idea remains responsible oversight.

This noun means a lover—a person who is loved in a romantic or intimate sense. It identifies the person connected with love or desire, rather than describing the feeling itself. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 17 times, including passages in Jeremiah, Lamentations, Ezekiel, Hosea, and Wisdom. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic reference remains a lover or beloved person.

This word means “wool” or “woolen,” referring to material made from the fleece of sheep. As a noun, it names the material itself rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Ezekiel 44:17. The word’s basic sense is therefore concrete and straightforward: it identifies wool or something made of wool. Its precise role in that verse depends on the surrounding context, which is not included here.

Esoba is a proper name, referring to a person named Esoba, also rendered Esova. It is not presented here as a word describing an action, quality, object, or relationship; it functions as an identifying personal name. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 4:21. The available information identifies the name and its occurrence, but does not provide further meaning or background about the person. Its precise significance in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and genealogy.

Esria, also written Ezria, is a proper name rather than a common word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Ezra 7:3. Because it is a personal name, its ordinary meaning is its identification of a particular person in the biblical record, not a general concept to apply elsewhere. The surrounding verse would be needed to identify the person and understand the name’s specific role there.

gl: good habit of body; good state of health
d: good habit of body; good state of health

e.t: This noun refers to a “good habit of body” or a “good state of health”—a condition of physical well-being and sound bodily health. It describes health as an established, favorable condition rather than a single moment of feeling well. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in Sirach 30:15. The surrounding verse would be needed to explain how this idea functions in that specific passage.

This noun means reverence: a respectful, worshipful regard directed toward God. It describes an inward attitude that recognizes God’s worth and responds to him with honor rather than careless disregard. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish writings, the word occurs 56 times, showing that reverence is a recurring concern across this corpus. Its precise expression depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains humble respect before God.

Zambina, also known as Zamvina, is a proper name used to identify a person rather than describe an action, quality, or object. Its lexical meaning is therefore the name itself, not a broader concept or general word. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Ezra 10:43. The surrounding verse text is needed to explain the person’s specific role there.

This proper name identifies the people called “Ēlamaioi; Ilamei.” It is a group name rather than a description of an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Ezra 4:9, and its role there is to identify a people among those named. The available information establishes the group’s name and its use as a proper noun, but does not provide the surrounding verse text for further contextual detail.

This noun means “amazement”—a powerful response of astonishment or wonder. It names the condition of being deeply struck by something remarkable, rather than an action or a person. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs six times across six verses, including passages in 1 Samuel, Ecclesiastes, Ezekiel, and Song of Songs. Its precise force in any one passage depends on what produces the amazement in that surrounding context.

This LXX word is a proper name, given in the gloss as “Thekōitēs; Thekitis.” It identifies a person or named individual rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. The word occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament corpus: once in 2 Samuel 23:26 and once in 1 Chronicles 27:9. Without the surrounding verse text, its specific reference cannot be described further, but its basic function is to designate a named person.

This noun means “slaughter”: the violent killing of people or animals. It names an act or scene of killing rather than describing a person who performs it. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 13 times, including passages in Numbers, 2 Samuel, Psalms, and Wisdom. Its central sense remains direct and grave wherever it appears, while the surrounding verse determines who is killed and what circumstances lead to the slaughter.

Jasper is the name of a gemstone. As a noun in the Greek Old Testament, it identifies this particular precious stone rather than an action, quality, or person. The word occurs four times, in Exodus, Isaiah, and Ezekiel, showing its use in descriptions of valuable or ornamental stones. Its precise significance in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

Ieser is a proper name, referring to a particular person rather than describing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek LXX, it appears once, at Numbers 26:49. The available meaning is limited to the name itself, so the name alone does not identify the person’s role or significance. Its precise reference is understood from the surrounding passage in Numbers.

This word is a proper name, rendered as “Iōchēl” or “Iokhil.” It identifies a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in the genealogical records of 1 Chronicles, at 1 Chronicles 2:34 and 2:35. The name’s precise identity and significance depend on the surrounding genealogical passage, but its basic function is to designate an individual by name.

This word means “by what” and functions as an adverb that asks about the means or basis involved in an action or event. In ordinary English, it points toward the thing through which something is done or comes about. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), it occurs once, at Leviticus 9:5. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, which is not included here.

This Greek Old Testament noun means “vault,” referring to a curved or arched covering or structure. It names a physical feature rather than an action or quality. The word appears once in the Greek Old Testament, in Isaiah 40:22, so its precise force there belongs to that verse’s surrounding description. Its basic sense remains a vaulted or arched form. This is an LXX word and should be understood as distinct from similarly rendered words in the Hebrew text or Greek New Testament.

This Greek LXX verb means “cast down” or “lay down”—to bring something or someone downward or place it down. It can describe a physical action, such as putting something down, and may also express the act of throwing or forcing something downward. The word occurs 43 times in the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical books represented here, so its precise force depends on what is being brought down and the surrounding sentence. Its basic idea remains movement from a higher position to a lower one.

This verb means “recline” or “lay down.” In the Greek Old Testament, it describes someone positioning the body down, whether resting, lying, or being placed in that position. It occurs seven times across six verses, including passages in Exodus, Numbers, Judges, 1 Samuel, and Daniel, as well as 3 Maccabees. Its exact force in a sentence depends on who is lying down and why, but the central idea remains moving into a reclining or lying position.

This Greek Old Testament noun means “distribution into bodies”: arranging people into separate groups or divisions. It refers to an organized partition rather than a random scattering. The word appears five times in the Greek Old Testament, all in Chronicles, where its use is connected with arranging people according to their divisions or assigned groups. Its basic sense is therefore the formal grouping or distribution of persons into bodies. The exact force in any one verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the central idea remains organized division.

This verb means to live wantonly—to behave in an uncontrolled, self-indulgent way. It describes a life marked by excess rather than restraint, and can be rendered “live wantonly” or “wanton.” In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, in Proverbs and Amos. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and larger context, but its central idea is reckless, undisciplined living. The word presents wanton behavior as an ongoing manner of life, not merely a single careless action.

This noun means “theft”: the taking of what belongs to someone else without permission. It names the wrongful act itself rather than the person who commits it. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, the word occurs six times, describing theft as a recognizable form of wrongdoing. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This LXX noun means “crystal,” referring to a clear, hard, shining substance. It names a material rather than an action, quality, or person. The word occurs nine times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical writings, including passages in Numbers, Job, Psalms, Isaiah, and Sirach. Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains crystal.

This noun means “conception,” referring to the beginning of pregnancy when a child is conceived. It names the act or event of becoming pregnant rather than describing the entire period of pregnancy or the birth itself. In the Greek Old Testament, this word occurs once, in Ruth 4:13. Its precise emphasis in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself has this clear, focused meaning.

This noun means “southwest wind,” naming a wind associated with that direction. It refers to a natural movement of air rather than a person, object, or action. The word appears 45 times in the Greek Old Testament text, across 38 verses, so it is used repeatedly for directional or weather-related description. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense remains a southwest wind.

This Greek Old Testament noun means “border of a robe,” referring to the edge or finished boundary of a garment. It is used for clothing connected with the tabernacle and priestly garments, especially in descriptions of how those garments were made. The word occurs seven times in the Greek Old Testament, all in Exodus, across six verses. Its meaning remains focused and concrete: the robe’s border or edge, rather than the whole garment or a separate item of clothing.

Madan, also rendered Mathan, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a person in the Old Testament genealogical record. The name appears twice in the Greek Old Testament, in Genesis 25:2 and 1 Chronicles 1:32. Since no further definition or verse text is provided, its ordinary significance here is its role as an individual’s name, while the surrounding genealogy identifies the person more specifically.

This adverb means “far away” or “lengthy,” describing something extended in distance or extent. It can point to remoteness—something located at a considerable distance—or to something stretched out or prolonged. The word occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical writings, including passages in Deuteronomy, Jeremiah, and Wisdom. Its precise force in any one verse depends on what it modifies and the surrounding sentence, but its central idea is distance or extended length.

This noun means “lad” or “stripling,” referring to a young male person. It is a straightforward term for someone youthful, without requiring a special spiritual or symbolic meaning. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs twice, both times in 4 Maccabees. The precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and its description of the person, but the word itself identifies him as a young man or youth.

Melchisoue is a proper name, referring to a particular person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. It appears three times in the Greek Old Testament, all in 1 Chronicles, and is rendered in the lexical record as “Melchisoue” or “Melkhisue.” The available references are 1 Chronicles 8:33, 9:39, and 10:2. Because no verse text or surrounding context is provided here, the individual’s role must be understood from those passages rather than from the name alone.

This Greek LXX verb means to partake or share—to take part in something or receive a portion with others. It describes participation rather than merely observing, and its precise emphasis depends on what a person is sharing or receiving in the sentence. The word occurs 13 times in the deuterocanonical Greek LXX books represented here, including Wisdom and 2–4 Maccabees. Its central idea remains active participation in, or sharing of, something with others.

This noun means “taint” or “defilement,” referring to something that makes a person, object, or situation unclean. It names the condition of impurity rather than the act that produces it. In the Greek LXX writings, it occurs four times, across Leviticus, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and 1 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse, but its central meaning remains a stain or defiling condition.

This adjective means “by night” or “nightly,” describing something that takes place during the nighttime. It identifies a time or setting rather than naming a person, object, or action by itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs six times, all in verses from Job, Psalms, and Proverbs. The word’s basic sense remains focused on what belongs to or happens during the night; the surrounding verse determines exactly what nighttime activity or condition it describes.

This noun refers to a builder or architect—someone who constructs buildings or oversees their construction. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used for people involved in building work, including builders serving in royal and temple repairs. The word appears seven times across seven verses, so its basic sense remains focused and concrete rather than describing a broad spiritual quality. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage and the building activity being discussed.

This adjective describes something serving as instruments—something used in an instrumental or tool-like capacity. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, at 2 Maccabees 12:15. The basic idea is functional: it points to something that serves as a means or instrument rather than naming the person or action using it. Its exact force in that verse depends on the surrounding sentence and context.

This word means “oath,” a noun referring to a formally stated promise or commitment. It is used throughout the Greek Old Testament and related writings, including passages involving personal promises, sworn commitments, and obligations. The word occurs 53 times in the Greek LXX corpus, showing that it regularly describes an oath rather than an action or emotion. Its precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding words and situation.

This Greek adverb means “again,” expressing a repeated action, event, or return. It tells the reader that something happens another time or that someone turns back to a former place or condition. In the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, it occurs 71 times, showing that repetition and renewed action are common uses. The word appears from Genesis through 4 Maccabees, but its basic meaning remains consistent: what happened before is happening once more, or what was previously left is being revisited.

gl: behave ill at wine; play drunken tricks
d: behave ill at wine; play drunken tricks

e.t: This Greek LXX verb describes behaving badly under the influence of wine—playing drunken tricks. It refers to unruly or foolish conduct associated with drinking, rather than simply mentioning wine itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Isaiah 41:12. The surrounding verse text is not included here, so the word’s precise force in that passage must be understood from its context.

gl: shut in all round; surround on all sides
d: shut in all round; surround on all sides

e.t: This Greek Old Testament verb means “shut in all round” or “surround on all sides.” It describes an action that encloses something completely, leaving it hemmed in by surrounding boundaries or forces. As a verb, it expresses what someone or something does rather than naming the enclosure itself. It occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, in Job 30:4, so its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. The central idea remains complete enclosure or being shut in from every side.

This adjective describes someone deeply overwhelmed by grief or sorrow—someone who is grief-stricken. It expresses an intense emotional condition rather than a mild moment of sadness. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs five times, including passages in Genesis, Psalms, and Daniel. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage, but its central idea remains a person weighed down by profound sorrow.

This Greek LXX noun means “cooking,” referring to the preparation of food by heat. It names an activity rather than a person, object, or quality. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament represented here, in Hosea 7:4. Because the verse text and surrounding context are not included, its exact force in that passage cannot be described further, but its basic meaning remains the act or process of cooking. This is a specific, practical term connected with preparing food.

This Greek LXX noun refers to fullness or a throng—a large, gathered multitude. It can describe people viewed together as a full crowd rather than as separate individuals. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 3 Maccabees 4:17, so its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. Its central idea remains a sense of abundance or a gathered company, with the context determining whether the emphasis falls more naturally on fullness or on the multitude itself.

This Greek LXX noun means “doing,” referring to an action or something carried out. It presents activity as an accomplished or performed deed, rather than merely an idea or intention. The word has 153 occurrences in the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical corpus, showing that it is used broadly for the performance of something. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding wording and subject.

This word means “prayer”: an address to God made by someone seeking, asking, or speaking before him. It is a noun, naming prayer rather than describing the act with a verb. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 88 times, showing that prayer is a recurring subject in passages such as Psalms, Kings, and Chronicles. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding words, but its central meaning remains prayer directed toward God.

This verb means to stretch forth—to extend something outward or reach it forward. It describes an action rather than an object, so the surrounding sentence identifies what is being extended or toward what it is directed. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs seven times, all in the deuterocanonical books, especially 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central idea remains deliberate extension or reaching outward.

This verb means “grow feathers.” It describes the development of feathers, using an action word rather than naming the feathers themselves. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Isaiah 40:31. The word’s precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains the act of growing feathers. This is a specific and vivid word for becoming feathered or developing plumage, rather than a general term for growth.

Riphath is a proper name, also rendered Rhifath. It identifies a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, the name occurs twice: once in Genesis and once in 1 Chronicles. Both occurrences use the rendering “Riphath.” The name’s precise significance cannot be determined from the name alone, but its function is clear: it serves as a personal designation in biblical genealogical material.

Sara is a proper name—the personal name of a woman in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies the same person named Sara throughout the passages where it occurs, rather than describing a quality, action, or general object. The name appears 20 times in the Greek Old Testament, across 16 verses, beginning in Genesis and appearing later in Numbers and Joshua. Its meaning here is therefore simply the personal name “Sara.”

This word is a Greek LXX proper name, referring to a person named “Sennachērim” or “Sennakhirim.” It is not a common noun describing an action, quality, or object, but a name used to identify one individual in the biblical narrative. The name occurs 16 times in the Greek LXX corpus, appearing in both Old Testament and deuterocanonical books. Its precise significance in any particular passage comes from the surrounding text, while its basic lexical function remains that of a personal name.

This word means “warped” or “crooked.” As an adjective, it describes something bent, twisted, or not straight; as a noun, it can refer to what is crooked. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used 22 times, mostly in the Old Testament books and especially Proverbs. Its central idea can apply to a physical shape or to something morally or figuratively distorted, depending on the sentence. The exact force in any verse comes from the surrounding words and context.

Some is a proper name used to identify an individual in the Greek Old Testament (LXX). It is rendered “Some,” rather than functioning as the ordinary English word meaning an unspecified amount or group. This name occurs three times in the LXX corpus, appearing twice in Genesis and once in 1 Chronicles. Without the surrounding verse text, the particular person and context cannot be described further.

This word refers to flax or tow, the loose, fibrous material prepared from flax and used as something that can be twisted, tied, or burned. It can function as a noun for the material itself and may also describe something made of it. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs five times, including passages in Judges, Isaiah, Daniel, and Sirach. Its ordinary sense remains focused on a fragile plant fiber or bundle of such fibers.

This Greek LXX verb means “tread together; trample under foot.” It describes the action of pressing down on something by walking over it, with the wording emphasizing forceful trampling. The verb occurs four times in the Greek Old Testament represented here, all in 2 Kings. Its precise force in any one passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains the physical act of stepping on and crushing or overpowering something underfoot.

This LXX Greek word describes something advantageous or beneficial, and it can also express bringing things or people together. As a verb, it may describe what produces a useful result; as an adjective, it identifies what is beneficial or fitting. It occurs 11 times in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books, including passages in Deuteronomy, Proverbs, Esther, Jeremiah, and Sirach. Its precise sense in any particular verse depends on how the surrounding sentence uses the idea.

This adjective expresses something at an “extremity” or describes it as “completely.” It can therefore point to the furthest limit of something or emphasize that nothing is lacking in its completeness. In the Greek LXX, it occurs once, in 3 Maccabees 1:22. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, which are not included here. The word’s basic sense remains focused on an extreme point or complete condition.

This noun means “delightfulness”—the quality of being pleasing, enjoyable, or delightful. It describes something that brings glad appreciation rather than burden or displeasure. In the Greek Old Testament corpus, the word appears twice, both times in Psalms. Its exact emphasis in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its central idea remains the pleasing or delightful character of a person, thing, or experience.

This adjective means “quality; such,” describing something according to its kind or character. It points to what something is like, rather than naming the thing itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Ezra 5:3, so its precise force there depends on the surrounding sentence and passage. Its basic function remains a concise description of the kind or quality being discussed.

This noun refers to a table, a flat piece of furniture or surface, and can also mean a bank, such as the side of a river. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings, its main sense is “table,” including tables used for ordinary purposes and sacred service. It occurs 77 times in this LXX corpus, so its exact meaning depends on the sentence where it appears.

Tobias, also rendered Tovias, is a proper name used for people in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical writings. It identifies an individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. This name appears five times in the Greek Old Testament corpus, including passages in 2 Chronicles, Nehemiah, and 2 Maccabees. The name itself does not provide the surrounding person’s role or character; those details must come from the passage where it occurs.

This verb means to surpass something or to overstep a boundary, limit, or expected measure. It describes going beyond what is normally allowed, required, or reached. In the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical writings represented here, it occurs six times, including passages in Sirach, 2 Maccabees, and 3 Maccabees. The surrounding sentence determines whether the emphasis is on exceeding a standard or crossing a limit.

Pharathōni, also rendered Farathoni, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a person or place by name in the Greek Old Testament tradition, but the available lexical information does not specify which. This name occurs once in the LXX corpus, at 1 Chronicles 11:31. Its exact identification depends on the surrounding verse and passage, which are not included here.

Phē is a noun presented as “Phē,” rather than as an English concept or descriptive action. The available lexical information gives no broader definition beyond this designation, so its ordinary meaning cannot be expanded safely. In the Greek Old Testament corpus, it occurs once, at Psalms 118:129. That single reference identifies where the word appears, but without the verse text it does not establish any additional contextual meaning or significance. Its precise force therefore belongs to the surrounding passage and cannot be explained further from the lexical information alone.

This word means “Chasalōth” or “Khasaloth”. It functions as a proper name rather than as a general description or action word. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, at Joshua 19:18. The name identifies a specific named subject, so its meaning is the name itself, not a quality, command, or spiritual concept. Because it has no broader usage in this corpus, its precise significance depends on the surrounding passage.

This word means “commander,” referring to a person who holds authority over others, especially in an organized military or civic setting. It is a noun naming the person rather than describing an action. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish writings represented by this LXX corpus, it occurs 27 times, including passages involving recognized leaders among Israel’s tribes, armies, or officials. Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage and the role assigned to that commander.

This Greek LXX noun means “secret door,” referring to a concealed or hidden entrance. It names a physical feature rather than an action, person, or abstract idea. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in Bel and the Dragon 1:15. Its precise significance in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and narrative, but its basic meaning remains a door or entrance kept out of ordinary view.

This word means “flax” or “raw rough cloth”. It is a noun referring to the plant fiber or to coarse, unfinished material made from it. The term appears once in the Greek Old Testament translation, in Sirach 40:4, and its precise role there depends on the surrounding verse text. Its basic sense points to a simple, rough textile rather than finished clothing or finely prepared fabric.

“With ears cut off” describes someone or an animal whose ears have been cut away or removed. It is an adjective, identifying a physical condition rather than an action or a person’s character. In the Greek Old Testament, this word occurs twice, both times in Leviticus. Its central meaning is precise and physical: the ears are missing because they have been cut off.
